entities.name: Joaquín Gutkeled
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Joaquín Gutkeled, a powerful Hungarian lord from the distinguished Gutkeled kindred, emerged as a central, destabilizing force in the Hungarian Kingdom during the tumultuous latter half of the 13th century. His actions, particularly the audacious kidnapping of the young Prince Ladislaus in 1272, critically undermined the already fragile authority of the Árpád dynasty, plunging the realm into an era known as "feudal anarchy." This period of intense baronial infighting and royal impotence fundamentally reshaped the political landscape of medieval Hungary, setting precedents for decentralization and the rise of powerful provincial magnates.

His most notorious act occurred in June 1272, when he seized Prince Ladislaus, the ten-year-old son and heir of King Stephen V, and imprisoned him in his fortress of Kőszeg. This unprecedented act of defiance by a baron against the reigning monarch sent shockwaves through the kingdom and served as a catalyst for a prolonged period of internal strife. Gutkeled, along with other ambitious noble families like the Kőszegis and Csáks, frequently switched allegiances, engaging in armed conflicts and forming unstable factions that continuously challenged the crown and each other for control of territories and royal offices. His strategies often involved exploiting the weakness of the monarchy to aggrandize his own regional power base, particularly in the western and northern marches of Hungary.

entities.name: Joaquín Gutkeled
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Joaquín Gutkeled (died April 1, 1277), a formidable magnate from the powerful Gutkeled kindred, became a pivotal and disruptive force in the Kingdom of Hungary during the tumultuous third quarter of the 13th century. His audacious actions, most notably the kidnapping of the young Prince Ladislaus in June 1272, irrevocably destabilized the Árpád dynasty's waning authority and effectively initiated a half-century of acute aristocratic infighting, subsequently termed the "feudal anarchy." Operating primarily from his stronghold in Slavonia and wielding immense territorial influence, Gutkeled embodied the ascendant "provincial lord" whose ambitions directly challenged the royal prerogative, fundamentally transforming Hungary's political landscape from a centralized monarchy into a fragmented realm dominated by powerful oligarchs.

Gutkeled's ascent to power was marked by a relentless pursuit of territorial consolidation and political leverage. After King Stephen V's death in August 1272, largely precipitated by the scandal of Ladislaus's abduction, Joaquín Gutkeled became a leading figure in the ongoing power struggles against rival baronial factions, particularly the Kőszegi and Csák families. He served multiple terms as Ban of Slavonia (1272–1273, 1274–1275, 1276) and concurrently held the office of Judge Royal in 1275, accumulating vast wealth and military resources. His control over key fortresses, including Koprivnica and Zagreb, allowed him to exert considerable influence over the southern and western regions of the kingdom, often engaging in border skirmishes with neighboring duchies and asserting a semi-independent authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Joaquín Gutkeled's actions, especially the kidnapping of Prince Ladislaus, were a direct catalyst for the "feudal anarchy" that fragmented Hungary's central authority for fifty years. This period fundamentally reshaped Hungarian governance, accelerating the decline of the Árpád dynasty and ushering in an era of powerful regional oligarchs.
